```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# --- CONFIGURATION ---
# Set the name of the target distribution matching your simulation[cite: 5]
TARGET_DIST <- "binomial" 

# Adjust output directory path to match where your files were written[cite: 5]
data_dir <- "~/SJSU26F/MATH167R/CLT/data/binomial"

# Load saved simulation dataset and add necessary columns for tables[cite: 5]
summary_table <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "binom_metrics.csv")) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_bias = sim_mean - theo_mean,
    se_ratio = sim_se / theo_se
  )
```

## 1. Original Population Distribution

<!-- Question 1: What does the original population distribution look like? -->

- **Name / Class:** `r TARGET_DIST`
- **Type:** Discrete, unimodal, right-skewed
- **Description:**
  <!-- Describe features: continuity, boundedness, symmetry/skewness, support, unimodal vs multimodal, etc. -->
  This is a discrete distribution with numbers between 0 and 5. It is
  strongly right-skewed, unimodal (one peak) and narrowly dispersed.
  This means that there is high likelihood the number generated will be
  0.

```{r}
#| label: fig-population-shape
#| fig-cap: "Theoretical / baseline shape of the population distribution (n = 1)."

ggplot(data.frame(x = c(0, 5)), aes(x = x)) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dbinom,
    args = list(size = 5, prob = 0.1),
    geom = "col",       # Changes the default line to columns
    n = 6,              # CRITICAL: Forces evaluation at exactly 6 points (0 to 5)
    fill = "#CC79A7", 
    color = "black", 
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:5) + # Explicitly set integer ticks
  labs(
    title = paste("Population Mass:", TARGET_DIST),
    x = "Successes",
    y = "Probability"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Theoretical Mean and Standard Deviation

- **Theoretical Mean (**$\mu$): 0.5\[cite: 5\]
- **Theoretical Standard Deviation (**$\sigma$):
  `r round(sqrt(5 * 0.1 * 0.9), 4)`\[cite: 5\]

For a Binomial distribution bounded by the number of trials
$n_{\text{size}} = 5$ and probability $p = 0.10$, the PMF is:

$$P(X = k) = \binom{n_{\text{size}}}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n_{\text{size}}-k}$$

The theoretical mean is calculated as:

$$\mu = n_{\text{size}} \cdot p = 5(0.10) = 0.5$$

The theoretical standard deviation is derived from the variance:

$$\sigma = \sqrt{n_{\text{size}} \cdot p \cdot (1-p)} = \sqrt{5(0.10)(0.90)} = \sqrt{0.45} \approx 0.6708$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Rate of Convergence to Normality

<!-- Question 3: How quickly does the sampling distribution become approximately normal? -->

- **Observations across sample sizes (**$n$):
  <!-- At what sample size n does skewness drop close to 0? Kurtosis near 0? -->
  In the graph shown below we can see that kurtosis is relatively stable
  from a lower sample size. As the sample size grows, skewness decreases
  and approaches a nominal amount.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shape-statistics
#| fig-cap: "Convergence of Skewness and Excess Kurtosis toward zero as sample size increases."

summary_table %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(skewness, excess_kurtosis), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = value, color = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("skewness" = "#CC79A7", "excess_kurtosis" = "blue")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Shape Statistics vs. n for", TARGET_DIST),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "Metric Value",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Simulated Mean vs. Theoretical Mean

<!-- Question 4: How does the simulated mean compare with the theoretical mean? -->
The simulated mean and theoretical mean show us if our Monte Carlo
simulation model is behaving as expected.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mean-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of simulated sample means vs. theoretical mean."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, theo_mean, sim_mean, mean_bias) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Theoretical Mean (μ)", "Simulated Mean (X̄)", "Mean Bias (X̄ - μ)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Analysis:**
  <!-- Does the empirical mean stay close to the theoretical mean across all n? Is there any noticeable bias? -->
  A relatively low bias throughout all sample sizes shows that the model
  is predicting correctly and there is not a large amount of bias.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Simulated Standard Error vs. Theoretical Standard Error

<!-- Question 5: How does the simulated standard error compare with SE(X̄) = σ / √n? -->

$$\text{SE}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-se-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of simulated standard errors with theoretical SE = σ / √n."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, theo_se, sim_se, se_ratio) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Theoretical SE", "Simulated SE", "SE Ratio (Sim / Theo)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Analysis:**
  <!-- Does the ratio sim_se / theo_se remain close to 1.0? Does the empirical spread decay at rate 1 / √n? -->
  The theoretical standard error and simulated standard error ratio
  remains very close to 1 throughout the sample size changes which shows
  that the simulation is an ideal benchmark we are able to draw
  conclusions from.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Evidence for Normality

<!-- Question 6: What evidence supports your conclusion that the distribution is—or is not—approximately normal? -->

### Graphical Evidence (Density & Q-Q Plots)

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-dist-qq
#| fig-cap: "Standardized empirical density and Normal Q-Q plots across selected sample sizes $n$ ($B = 10{,}000$)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-align: "center"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(8676)

B <- 10000L
selected_n <- c(1, 10, 20, 25)
binom_size <- 5L
binom_prob <- 0.10

density_qq_list <- list()

for (n_val in selected_n) {
  observations <- rbinom(B * n_val, size = binom_size, prob = binom_prob)
  sample_matrix <- matrix(observations, nrow = B, ncol = n_val)
  means <- rowMeans(sample_matrix)
  
  sim_mean <- mean(means)
  sim_se <- sd(means)
  
  z_means <- if (is.finite(sim_se) && sim_se > 0) (means - sim_mean) / sim_se else rep(NA_real_, B)
  density_qq_list[[length(density_qq_list) + 1]] <- data.frame(
    n_label = paste0("n = ", n_val),
    n_num = n_val,
    z = z_means
  )
}

plot_data <- bind_rows(density_qq_list) %>% filter(is.finite(z))
plot_data$n_label <- factor(plot_data$n_label, levels = paste0("n = ", selected_n))

tight_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 4, r = 6, b = 4, l = 6)
  )

p_dens_tight <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = z)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#CC79A7", alpha = 0.35, color = "#CC79A7", linewidth = 0.6) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ n_label, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Empirical Density vs N(0,1)", x = "Standardized Mean (Z)", y = "Density") +
  tight_theme

p_qq_tight <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(sample = z)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray30") +
  stat_qq(color = "#CC79A7", alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ n_label, nrow = 2) +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plots", x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Sample Quantiles") +
  tight_theme

p_dens_tight | p_qq_tight
```

- **Density Overlays:**
  <!-- Mention the alignment with the standard N(0, 1) curve. --> As
  seen in the density charts, the discrete nature of the graph forces
  many peaks through the distribution. As the sample size increases we
  can start to see the graph become smoother. There is quite a large
  difference between n = 24 and n = 25 visually.
- **Q-Q Plot Quantile Alignment:**
  <!-- Inspect the linearity in your Q-Q plots. --> While there are
  steps due to the discrete nature of the binomial distribution, the Q-Q
  plots are linear enough through the sample sizes.

### Statistical Evidence (Shapiro-Wilk Test & Moment Ratios)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-normality-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Normality assessment metrics: Skewness, Kurtosis, and Shapiro-Wilk test."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, skewness, excess_kurtosis, shapiro_W, shapiro_p) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Skewness", "Excess Kurtosis", "Shapiro-Wilk W", "p-value")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Conclusion on Normality:**
  <!-- Summarize when the distribution meets practical and formal normality thresholds. -->
  Statistically we can see the decrease in skewness from a starting
  value of 1.188 (n = 1) to 0.203 at (n = 25). Kurtosis stays relatively
  stable around 0 after the first couple sampling size increases. The
  Shapiro-Wilk W value also approaches 1 very quickly indicating that
  the practical shape of the distribution is becoming normal. The reason
  this is not reflected in the p-value is because the binomials discrete
  nature creates micro-steps that only start to smooth when the sample
  size reaches very large amounts. The sample size n = 25 is when these
  three values start to align, skewness decreases, kurtosis stays normal
  and while the W value in my simulation actually decreases it still
  remains around 1.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Limitations and Surprises

<!-- Question 7: What limitations or surprises did you observe? -->

- **Key Observations / Surprises:**
  <!-- e.g., persistent tail skewness, boundary effects, Shapiro-Wilk p-value sensitivity to large sample sizes, etc. -->
  The key observation I noticed was the affect the discrete nature of
  the binomial distribution had on the sample means. The sample
  distribution remained very peaked until sample sizes started to get
  into the 20's.
- **Simulation Limitations:**
  <!-- e.g., finite Monte Carlo reps B = 10,000, fixed selection of n_values, truncation of sub-sample size for normality testing. -->
  I noticed with some experimentation that the lower Monte Carlo reps
  generated smoother graphs, and that larger rep sizes generated graphs
  that remained pointed throughout the sample size increases.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Final Verdict

#### Central Limit Theorem Confirmed at *n = 25*

<!-- Final thoughts on convergence --> The binomial distribution
presents an interesting challenge because the Shapiro-Wilk statistic
approaches 1 rapidly indicating a normal distribution shape but visually
this is not confirmed until around n = 25. The decision to choose n = 25
over n = 20 was purely because of the peaks still being very visible as
well as the skewness value indicating a right skew.
